title: Leonid meteor shower
content:
DECATUR, Ill. (WAND) – Bundle up, find a dark spot and look up: The annual Leonid meteor shower is back, bringing a chance to catch some of the fastest “shooting stars” of the year.

In 2026, the Leonids are expected to peak on the night of November 17 into the early morning of November 18. You may also spot a few meteors on surrounding nights. The best viewing is generally after midnight and before dawn, when the constellation Leo climbs higher in the sky.

Under dark skies, observers might see around 15 meteors per hour near the peak. That’s an idealized estimate, not a guarantee: Light pollution, clouds and the height of the shower’s radiant all affect what you’ll actually see. This year, the first-quarter moon is expected to set around midnight, leaving darker skies for the prime predawn viewing hours.

Where do the Leonids come from?

The Leonids appear when Earth passes through a trail of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Most of the particles are tiny, but when they slam into our atmosphere at roughly 44 miles per second, they heat the surrounding air and create the bright streaks we call meteors.

The shower gets its name from Leo the Lion: Trace the meteors’ paths backward and they appear to radiate from that constellation. But you don’t need to find Leo to enjoy the show. Meteors can appear anywhere in the sky, so a wide, open view is your best bet.

When is the comet’s next perihelion?

Tempel-Tuttle orbits the sun about once every 33 years. Its next perihelion—the point in its orbit closest to the sun—is expected on May 20, 2031. Its previous perihelion was in 1998.

The comet’s return is worth watching because the Leonids have a history of spectacular meteor storms. In 1966, observers in parts of North America saw thousands of meteors in a short period. But a comet’s return does not guarantee another storm: The display depends on whether Earth intersects a particularly dense trail of debris. For 2026, plan on a modest shower rather than a meteor storm.

How to watch

  • Choose a dark location away from streetlights, with a clear view of as much sky as possible.
  • Go after midnight, especially in the hours before sunrise, and check your local cloud forecast first.
  • Give your eyes about 20–30 minutes to adjust to the dark; avoid looking at bright phone screens.
  • Bring a reclining chair and warm layers. November nights can be chilly, and patience pays off.
  • Skip the telescope. Your eyes are the best tool for watching a broad area of sky.

Even if the Leonids don’t deliver a storm this year, a quiet night under the stars—and the chance to see a streak of comet dust flash overhead—is reason enough to step outside.
